intro: I built a small transformer in PyTorch and trained it on Shakespeare because I wanted to understand what was happening inside a language model, not just be able to repeat the steps.
orientation: Then I built a visualizer around it, using the model's actual values to make those steps easier to follow.
origin: I'd been studying transformers and could kind of explain how tokens went through attention and eventually became an output. But knowing the order wasn't the same as understanding it. Residual connections were hard for me to picture, and I had the same problem with backpropagation and optimizers on the training side.

Karpathy's videos and 3Blue1Brown helped a lot. I followed the small GPT architecture Karpathy teaches, implemented it in PyTorch, and trained it on Tiny Shakespeare. I wasn't trying to build a better language model. I wanted something small enough that I could follow the computation myself.
residual: Residual connections were one of the things that started making more sense when I built it. Instead of replacing the existing values, a part of the model calculates an update and adds it back. Seeing the original values and the update together made that much easier for me to picture.
visualizer: Getting the model working was one thing. Figuring out how to show it was another. I had to break the computation into steps and make them flow into each other, including in 3D, without making the explanation wrong.

The model doesn't literally look like those animations. I had to choose a way to show it, but I didn't want to make up numbers just because they looked good. The core scenes use values captured from the model I actually trained.
training: The training side was part of it too. I wanted to understand how changing the weights changes the predictions, rather than treat training as something that just happens before you use the model.
takeaway: The biggest thing that clicked was the path from an input all the way to the probabilities for what comes next. Concepts that had felt separate started fitting together once I could follow the values through them.

That still isn't the same as being able to explain everything the model does. I can trace the computation, but understanding why it learned a particular representation is much harder. Building it made that distinction a lot clearer to me.
